full_text: BackgroundPaediatric asthma exhibits marked clinical heterogeneity and cannot be simply considered the childhood counterpart of adult asthma. Early-life environmental exposures can reshape immune-cell metabolic programs and potentially drive long-lasting inflammatory phenotypes. Existing explanatory frameworks for paediatric asthma largely centre on Th2-related inflammation, epithelial-alarm signalling and neuro-immune crosstalk, while the contributions of immunometabolic processes to disease endotypes remain under-summarised.ObjectiveThis review collates available evidence regarding metabolic reprogramming in the pathogenesis of paediatric asthma and provides an integrated immunometabolic perspective on this condition.ResultsSummarized evidence covers immunometabolic changes across key airway-resident and infiltrating cell populations. Discussion addresses core paediatric-specific biological features, including early-life developmental windows, virus-related trained immunity, obese asthma, circadian-sleep interactions, neuro-metabolic-immune communication and metabolomics-based endotyping. The framework is organized around substrate competition rather than a glycolysis-versus-OXPHOS binary, because Tregs, M2-like macrophages and pathogenic ILC2s share lipid and amino-acid pools but exert opposing functions. From these observations emerges a testable “Metabolic Latching Model” of how early-life insults establish persistent inflammatory memory through metabolism–epigenetic coupling, with “latching” operationally defined by exposure removal and persistence beyond responding-cell turnover. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) and the Treg-to-effector balance are placed at the centre of this framework. Three hypotheses are prioritised as feasible with current technology: H1 (monocyte glycolytic baseline predicting wheeze-to-asthma transition), H4 (metabolic intervention in obese asthma), and H6 (the HDAC2-GSH/butyrate axis in steroid sensitivity).ConclusionCurrent evidence suggests that immunometabolic reprogramming serves as one plausible contributing factor for the heterogeneity of paediatric asthma. This conceptual framework may bridge molecular metabolic findings and paediatric clinical contexts, and inform future mechanistic and clinical studies in this research area. 7.6Methodological toolboxSingle-cell layer: scRNA-seq plus metabolic pathway activity scoring with scMetabolism and flux inference from scFEA, combined with scATAC to lock metabolism–epigenome cell states, and spatial transcriptomics to localize metabolic subsets anatomically.Metabolite layer: targeted/untargeted LC-MS (blood, urine, EBC, BALF), lipidomics, and isotope tracing (13C-glucose/glutamine) as a direct flux measurement, distinct from the computational scores and inference above.Functional layer: Seahorse cell energy metabolism analysis, NAD(P)H and mitochondrial membrane potential live imaging, ferroptosis probes (C11-BODIPY).Model layer: air-liquid interface epithelial organoids, macrophage-epithelium-microbiota co-culture, organoid-on-chip exposure to viruses/pollutants; Computational layer: machine-learning multi-omic endotyping and digital-twin-style metabolic flux modeling (COBRA/flux balance).Clinical layer: nested metabolomic sub-studies in birth cohorts, metabolic dynamics sampling around viral challenge tests, and chronopharmacology designs with circadian-phase sampling. 8ConclusionStudies of paediatric asthma are exploring perspectives beyond describing over-expressed-cytokines, toward investigating persistently-altered cellular-metabolic-programmes. A metabolic-reprogramming-oriented conceptual framework can integrate environmental-exposure-effects, microbiome-related influences, nutrition, circadian-biology and genetic susceptibility. It provides one plausible mechanistic explanation for how early-life-environmental-insults can shape later-childhood-disease-manifestations. Mechanistic themes including ferroptosis-related-pathways, mitochondrial-homeostasis, metabolic-origins of glucocorticoid-resistance and circadian-immunometabolic-coupling help connect molecular-level observations to paediatric clinical contexts. Children retain greater immune-metabolic-plasticity relative to adults. Metabolism-oriented-interventions may support endotype-remodelling, which may be harder to achieve in older-patient-populations. To move from synopsis to research programme, we nominate the first-wave studies described in Section 6 as feasible starting points that test the model’s central predictions with current technology. The “Metabolic Latching Model” together with its six derived-testable-hypotheses await further empirical assessment driven by advancing single-cell-multi-omics-technologies. 1Introduction: rationale for a metabolic perspective in paediatric asthmaThe global prevalence of paediatric asthma keeps rising, and patient manifestations vary greatly. Some children only have temporary wheeze triggered by viruses. Other children develop persistent severe disease that responds poorly to steroids (1). Traditional classification systems rely on Th2 status or eosinophil-neutrophil inflammation. These systems cannot fully explain disease diversity. They also cannot explain how early-life exposures lead to distinct inflammatory endotypes years later.Paediatric asthma is not a single disease but a set of trajectories. Longitudinal birth cohorts show that early-life wheeze partitions into distinct pathways: transient wheeze that resolves by school age, persistent wheeze that continues into adulthood, and late-onset wheeze (2, 3). Which pathway a child follows is the central clinical question, and it is precisely the question a metabolic framework must explain: the Metabolic Latching Model proposes, in part, that trajectory divergence reflects whether early-life metabolic-epigenetic latching is established, and whether it is later resolved (Section 6).Metabolic reprogramming means adaptive changes in cellular substrate use and energy metabolism after external stimulation. It is well documented in cancer research (4). Studies in immunometabolism show that immune cell function depends heavily on metabolic states. Metabolic intermediates can act as substrates for epigenetic modifiers. They form regulatory loops linking cell signals, metabolism and epigenetic modification. These loops may help explain how early-life environmental exposures contribute to asthma endotypes in children.Children have three important biological characteristics. First, a critical developmental window exists roughly from birth to six years old (2). Lung structure, immunity and metabolic homeostasis mature rapidly during this period. Metabolic disturbances in this window may cause long-lasting biological outcomes. Second, immune cell metabolism in children shows higher plasticity than in adults, an inference from the trained-immunity literature (Section 2.6) rather than a directly measured quantity, which itself marks how much basic paediatric immunometabolism remains unmeasured. This feature may create opportunities for early intervention. Third, childhood metabolic programming comes from both external environment and prenatal conditions. Prenatal nutrition, delivery mode and early feeding habits all play a role (Section 4.1).Direct human paediatric data on immunometabolism remain limited. For this reason, this review follows a clear structure. First, we introduce basic immunometabolic mechanisms shared across different age groups (Sections 2-3). Next, we describe how these pathways function under paediatric biological backgrounds (Section 4). Finally, we discuss the value and practical limits of metabolic-targeted therapies for children (Section 5). Many metabolic pathways work similarly across the lifespan. However, their modification in developmental windows can shape long-term asthma trajectories. This supports the value of studying paediatric asthma to understand asthma across age groups.The so-called “fourth dimension” of metabolic regulation works together with the classical Th2 inflammatory, epithelial-alarm and neuro-immune axes. It does not replace these existing frameworks. The neuro-metabolic-immune crosstalk described in Section 4.7 reflects metabolic adjustment of known neuro-immune signals. It is not an independent regulatory axis. The three classical axes mainly answer which cells produce inflammation. Metabolic signatures may help us understand why inflammation persists. Its explanatory value is greatest when it explains which cell wins under limiting substrate conditions—particularly ILC2s, Tregs and M2-like macrophages, which share lipid-oxidative and amino-acid-dependent programmes but exert opposing functions in paediatric asthma. Therefore, this review summarizes existing literature and puts forward a testable working model requiring further experimental verification (Section 6). 2General principles of immune cell metabolic reprogramming2.1Glycolysis versus oxidative phosphorylation: beyond simple binary classificationPro-inflammatory immune cells such as M1-like macrophages, Th1/Th17 cells and activated mast cells often use aerobic glycolysis, also known as the Warburg effect. This process is controlled by HIF-1α, mTOR and PI3K-Akt signals. In contrast, reparative or tolerogenic cells including M2-like macrophages, Treg cells and memory T cells tend to use fatty acid oxidation (FAO) and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). This general pattern has been repeatedly observed in asthma-related research (5). Still, several important points need consideration (6).Cell metabolic states form a continuous spectrum, not simple on-off switches. Many intermediate phenotypes exist between typical M1 and M2 states (Section 3.1). Glycolysis mainly supports biosynthesis and intracellular signal transmission. It is not only used for ATP production. For example, NADPH is generated mainly by the pentose phosphate pathway branching from glucose-6-phosphate, not by glycolysis per se. Succinate accumulation that stabilizes HIF-1α is a TCA-cycle event (7), demonstrated primarily in mouse and human macrophage models. Lactate acts both as a metabolic product and a signal molecule. Histone lactylation controlled by lactate can directly change gene transcription. This mechanism may support chronic airway inflammation (8). This lactate-dependent programme is also relevant to Treg biology: Foxp3 shifts Tregs away from Myc-driven glycolysis toward oxidative metabolism, allowing them to function in lactate-rich conditions that suppress effector T cells (Section 3.3).A caveat qualifies the glycolysis-versus-oxidative dichotomy throughout this review. Three populations with opposite roles in this disease, Tregs, M2-like macrophages and pathogenic ILC2s, converge on the same oxidative-lipid programme: Tregs run on lipid oxidation, alternatively activated macrophages depend on lipid uptake and lysosomal lipolysis, and ILC2s draw on the same fatty-acid pool for FAO and lipid-droplet formation (Section 3.2). The useful question is therefore which cell captures the substrate when fuel is limiting in an inflamed airway, a competition that pathway-preference data cannot answer and that carries direct consequences for the therapeutic logic of Section 5.2.2Lipid mediators: substrate competition in the arachidonic acid cascadeCells produce arachidonic acid after breaking down membrane phospholipids. This substance flows into LOX or COX pathways. These two sets of pathways balance the production of pro-inflammatory lipid mediators (leukotriene B4, cysteinyl leukotrienes) and pro-resolving lipid mediators (resolvins, protectins). Studies in asthma models report impaired cholesterol efflux controlled by ABCA1/G1 and foam-cell-like macrophage changes (6).Lipid mediators may serve as measurable markers of metabolic reprogramming. Lipidomic tests on exhaled breath condensate or induced sputum may reflect disease endotypes more stably than cytokine detection. This idea still needs full verification in paediatric patient cohorts.2.3Ferroptosis: potential effects of lipid metabolic changesFerroptosis is iron-dependent regulated cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation. Its core protective system includes the GPX4-glutathione (GSH) pathway. System Xc- cystine-glutamate exchanger and FSP1-CoQ10 pathway also provide protection (9, 10). Ferroptosis-related mechanisms may affect asthma in several ways.In airway epithelium, low GPX4 activity and excess lipid peroxidation may damage epithelial barriers and increase goblet cell metaplasia. Air pollutants such as PM2.5 and ozone can trigger epithelial ferroptosis in cell systems and animal models (11). In neutrophil-dominant inflammation, neutrophils face high redox pressure. NETosis shares partial mechanisms with ferroptosis, including lipid peroxidation and NADPH consumption; this mechanism is derived mainly from mouse and in vitro neutrophil studies, with human data limited to associations. The two processes may work together as terminal effector pathways.Studies of type-2 inflammation reveal a lymphocyte-related paradox. Type-2 innate and adaptive lymphocytes, rather than eosinophils, acquire ferroptosis tolerance as an active adaptation. Wientjens and colleagues showed that cystine uptake sustains glutathione synthesis in ILC2s and Th2 cells; GPX4 and TXNRD1 rise, ferroptosis tolerance follows, and lipid droplet accumulation is downstream of that tolerance. The tolerance itself facilitates pathogenic type-2 immunity in allergic airway inflammation (12). On the other side, experimental induction of eosinophil ferroptosis-like death enhances anti-inflammatory effects of glucocorticoids (13, 14). In arginine metabolism, iNOS produces NO while ARG1 produces ornithine. The two reactions compete for substrates. In tryptophan metabolism, the IDO-kynurenine pathway affects Treg function and nerve signal transmission. In glutaminolysis, metabolic flow supports TCA cycle supplementation and mTOR activity (15, 16).The tryptophan-kynurenine axis deserves attention in paediatric research. Gut microbiota strongly change tryptophan turnover. It forms a bridge connecting microbiome, metabolism and immunity (Section 4.4).2.5Mitochondrial quality control and inflammasomes: linking metabolic disturbance to inflammationMetabolic reprogramming cannot be separated from organelle homeostasis. It induces type-I interferon response and SASP-like cell status (17, 18).Respiratory viruses can interfere with mitophagy. This forms one molecular basis for trained immunity (21, 22).Transient stimuli such as RSV infection, low-dose LPS or BCG vaccination can trigger metabolic changes through mTOR/HIF-1α. Innate immune cells maintain enhanced response ability long after stimuli disappear (23, 24). Existing reviews have summarized the interaction between metabolism and epigenetics in trained immunity (24). full_text: RNA therapeutics have emerged as a promising and effective tool to treat a wide range of genetic, metabolic, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases by directly modulating the gene expression or directing transient protein production. Currently, more than 20 RNA-based drugs have been approved by the FDA, and due to their recent introduction into the clinical practice, long-term safety data remain limited and comparisons of adverse effects across platforms are lacking. This review focuses on the three major RNA therapeutic platforms, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNA (siRNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) and intends to provide a cross-platform analysis of their adverse effects. We searched studies published up to June 2026 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using terms related to RNA therapeutics, individual drug names, safety and toxicity outcomes. Clinical trials, extension studies, pharmacovigilance reports, regulatory documents, and prescribing information were considered for each FDA-approved ASO, siRNA and mRNA agent. The observed safety profiles are associated with an interaction between RNA modality and additional determinants, including chemical modification, delivery system, route of administration, biodistribution, target tissue, and clinical context. Innate immune activation represents a potential shared mechanism, whereas sequence-dependent off-target effects, delivery-associated reactions, administration-related complications, and organ-specific toxicities differ in relevance and mechanism among ASO, siRNA, and mRNA therapeutics. Although most reported adverse effects are mild to moderate, important research gaps regarding long-term safety, pediatric use and rare adverse effects still exist, underscoring the need for further optimization of RNA drug design and delivery technologies, as well as continued pharmacovigilance. 2MethodsThis review was conducted to summarize and compare the adverse effects associated with currently FDA-approved RNA therapeutics, including siRNAs, mRNA-based therapeutics and ASOs. We performed a literature search using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar databases for studies published up to June 2026. Search terms included combinations of “RNA therapeutics”, “RNA-based drugs”, “siRNA”, “antisense oligonucleotide”, “mRNA therapeutics”, “adverse effects”, “toxicity”, “safety” and the names of individual FDA-approved agents.Eligible sources included clinical trials, extension studies, observational studies, pharmacovigilance analyses, systematic reviews, regulatory documents from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) official websites, prescribing information, and relevant post-marketing safety reports. Publications not available in English, conference abstracts without sufficient safety data, duplicate reports, and preclinical studies without direct clinical relevance were excluded. For each therapeutic agent, information regarding approved indications, mechanism of action, route of administration, reported adverse effects, serious adverse reactions, and potential toxicity mechanisms was extracted. The collected data were organized according to therapeutic platform (siRNA, mRNA, and ASO therapeutics) and subsequently compared to identify common and distinct safety characteristics across RNA-based treatment modalities.For the purposes of this review, only FDA-approved agents belonging to the three prespecified modalities (siRNA, mRNA, and ASO) and falling within the review scope at the June 2026 cut-off were included. The included products, along with their approval year, indication, target, delivery system, route of administration, and safety characteristics, are summarized in Table 1. Regulatory and prescribing-information sources were used to establish approved indications and labeled safety information, while clinical trials and extension studies were used to characterize adverse-event patterns in defined study populations. Pharmacovigilance and post-marketing reports were interpreted primarily as sources of rare or emerging safety signals rather than as proof of causality.Because the included evidence sources differed in design, population, follow-up, and adverse-event reporting, no quantitative cross-study pooling or formal risk-of-bias grading was undertaken. When observations differed across evidence types, the terminology and causal interpretation of the original source were retained, and the strength and context of the evidence were considered qualitatively. No independent causality assessment of individual adverse events was performed. Events were described as adverse reactions only when the original clinical or regulatory source supported treatment attribution. full_text_sections.abstract: RNA therapeutics have emerged as a promising and effective tool to treat a wide range of genetic, metabolic, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases by directly modulating the gene expression or directing transient protein production. Currently, more than 20 RNA-based drugs have been approved by the FDA, and due to their recent introduction into the clinical practice, long-term safety data remain limited and comparisons of adverse effects across platforms are lacking. This review focuses on the three major RNA therapeutic platforms, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNA (siRNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) and intends to provide a cross-platform analysis of their adverse effects. We searched studies published up to June 2026 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using terms related to RNA therapeutics, individual drug names, safety and toxicity outcomes. Clinical trials, extension studies, pharmacovigilance reports, regulatory documents, and prescribing information were considered for each FDA-approved ASO, siRNA and mRNA agent. The observed safety profiles are associated with an interaction between RNA modality and additional determinants, including chemical modification, delivery system, route of administration, biodistribution, target tissue, and clinical context. Innate immune activation represents a potential shared mechanism, whereas sequence-dependent off-target effects, delivery-associated reactions, administration-related complications, and organ-specific toxicities differ in relevance and mechanism among ASO, siRNA, and mRNA therapeutics. Although most reported adverse effects are mild to moderate, important research gaps regarding long-term safety, pediatric use and rare adverse effects still exist, underscoring the need for further optimization of RNA drug design and delivery technologies, as well as continued pharmacovigilance.
full_text_sections.methods: 2MethodsThis review was conducted to summarize and compare the adverse effects associated with currently FDA-approved RNA therapeutics, including siRNAs, mRNA-based therapeutics and ASOs. We performed a literature search using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar databases for studies published up to June 2026. Search terms included combinations of “RNA therapeutics”, “RNA-based drugs”, “siRNA”, “antisense oligonucleotide”, “mRNA therapeutics”, “adverse effects”, “toxicity”, “safety” and the names of individual FDA-approved agents.Eligible sources included clinical trials, extension studies, observational studies, pharmacovigilance analyses, systematic reviews, regulatory documents from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) official websites, prescribing information, and relevant post-marketing safety reports. Publications not available in English, conference abstracts without sufficient safety data, duplicate reports, and preclinical studies without direct clinical relevance were excluded. For each therapeutic agent, information regarding approved indications, mechanism of action, route of administration, reported adverse effects, serious adverse reactions, and potential toxicity mechanisms was extracted. The collected data were organized according to therapeutic platform (siRNA, mRNA, and ASO therapeutics) and subsequently compared to identify common and distinct safety characteristics across RNA-based treatment modalities.For the purposes of this review, only FDA-approved agents belonging to the three prespecified modalities (siRNA, mRNA, and ASO) and falling within the review scope at the June 2026 cut-off were included. The included products, along with their approval year, indication, target, delivery system, route of administration, and safety characteristics, are summarized in Table 1. Regulatory and prescribing-information sources were used to establish approved indications and labeled safety information, while clinical trials and extension studies were used to characterize adverse-event patterns in defined study populations. Pharmacovigilance and post-marketing reports were interpreted primarily as sources of rare or emerging safety signals rather than as proof of causality.Because the included evidence sources differed in design, population, follow-up, and adverse-event reporting, no quantitative cross-study pooling or formal risk-of-bias grading was undertaken. When observations differed across evidence types, the terminology and causal interpretation of the original source were retained, and the strength and context of the evidence were considered qualitatively. No independent causality assessment of individual adverse events was performed. Events were described as adverse reactions only when the original clinical or regulatory source supported treatment attribution. Events with uncertain attribution were described as reported or observed adverse events without implying a direct causal relationship with the RNA therapeutic.Frequency descriptors such as “common” and “rare” were retained only when they were explicitly reported or defined by the source used for the corresponding product; otherwise, numerical frequencies or neutral descriptive wording were preferred. “Serious” refers to events classified as serious in the underlying clinical or regulatory source and should not be interpreted as synonymous with high frequency or proven drug causality.

full_text: Lysosomes are increasingly recognized as dynamic regulatory organelles that integrate degradation, nutrient sensing, lipid metabolism, membrane trafficking, and organelle quality control beyond their classical degradative functions. These activities are particularly important during lung development, when epithelial differentiation, alveolarization, lung maturation, surfactant homeostasis, and postnatal adaptation occur within a narrow developmental window. This review summarizes current evidence linking lysosome–autophagy networks to lung maturation, with emphasis on epithelial autophagy, alveolar type II (AT-II) cell function, lamellar-body biology, mitochondrial quality control, and alveolar macrophage regulation. We discuss how lysosomal lipid handling, autophagic flux, and mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR)–transcription factor EB (TFEB) signaling contribute to developmental homeostasis while distinguishing direct pulmonary evidence from mechanistic hypotheses derived from other systems. We further examine lysosomal and autophagic alterations in pediatric lung diseases, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia, cystic fibrosis, and viral respiratory infection, highlighting disease-specific upstream stressors and intracellular defects. Static autophagy markers cannot define functional flux, and conventional lysosomes must be distinguished from specialized lysosome-related organelles such as lamellar bodies. Finally, we discuss therapeutic opportunities and challenges, emphasizing cell-specific targeting, restoration of defined organelle defects, developmental safety, and rigorous functional validation. A developmentally informed understanding of lysosome–autophagy networks may provide new mechanistic frameworks for pediatric lung disease intervention. 5Conclusions and future perspectivesLysosomes occupy a central position at the interface of degradation, metabolism, organelle quality control, and inflammatory signaling in the developing lung. Direct pulmonary evidence supports epithelial autophagy in lung morphogenesis (7), AT-II cell autophagy-related pathways in lamellar-body maturation and surfactant homeostasis (8, 9), and the effects of experimentally altered lysosomal lipid handling on surfactant and alveolar structure (10). Disease-model studies identify context-dependent remodeling of autophagic or endolysosomal pathways in hyperoxic injury, BPD, and RSV infection (11, 19, 35, 36, 39, 40). These injury-related mechanisms should not be assumed to direct normal lung development.At the same time, the current evidence does not justify treating lysosomal dysfunction as a single uniform mechanism. The consequences of pathway perturbation depend on developmental stage, cell type, cargo, compartment, and the balance between lysosomal delivery and degradation. Static LC3-II or p62 measurements are insufficient to define flux, while pH measurements must specify the intracellular compartment. These methodological principles are essential for interpreting both experimental studies and future therapeutic trials.The most promising direction is therefore a developmentally informed, compartment-specific model of lysosomal biology. In this framework, lysosomes and lysosome-related organelles integrate metabolic and stress signals to maintain AT-II cell competence, surfactant homeostasis, mitochondrial quality, and immune function. When this adaptive network is disrupted by prematurity, hyperoxia, infection, or other stressors, impaired clearance, lipid imbalance, mitochondrial injury, and inflammatory amplification may contribute to defective alveolar and epithelial maturation. This model generates testable hypotheses without assuming that every pediatric lung phenotype is caused by a primary lysosomal defect.Future work should move from descriptive lysosomal phenotyping toward causal experiments that define the affected compartment and restore its function. Developmental timing, cell-specific delivery, dynamic flux measurements, organelle-resolved lipid and pH assays, and clinically relevant lung models will be particularly important. If these requirements are met, lysosome-centered biology may provide a tractable framework for understanding and eventually treating selected forms of pediatric lung disease. 1Background and overview of lysosome–autophagy networks in lung biologyThe overall organization of lysosome–autophagy networks in lung development and pediatric lung disease is summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Integrated lysosome–autophagy networks in lung development and pediatric lung disease.Illustration showing lung development from embryonic to postnatal stages, roles of the lysosome–autophagy network in autophagy, lipid handling, and mitochondrial quality control in AT-II cells, and how developmental or environmental stresses can disrupt these processes, causing pediatric lung injury.1.1Lysosomes as dynamic regulatory organelles beyond degradationLysosomes are acidic, single-membrane organelles containing a broad repertoire of hydrolases that degrade proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and other cellular cargo. Their function depends on coordinated luminal acidification, lysosome-associated membrane proteins 1 and 2 (LAMP1 and LAMP2), proton-pumping vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) complexes, and trafficking pathways that deliver endocytic and autophagic cargo to the degradative compartment (1–5). full_text_sections.abstract: Lysosomes are increasingly recognized as dynamic regulatory organelles that integrate degradation, nutrient sensing, lipid metabolism, membrane trafficking, and organelle quality control beyond their classical degradative functions. These activities are particularly important during lung development, when epithelial differentiation, alveolarization, lung maturation, surfactant homeostasis, and postnatal adaptation occur within a narrow developmental window. This review summarizes current evidence linking lysosome–autophagy networks to lung maturation, with emphasis on epithelial autophagy, alveolar type II (AT-II) cell function, lamellar-body biology, mitochondrial quality control, and alveolar macrophage regulation. We discuss how lysosomal lipid handling, autophagic flux, and mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR)–transcription factor EB (TFEB) signaling contribute to developmental homeostasis while distinguishing direct pulmonary evidence from mechanistic hypotheses derived from other systems. We further examine lysosomal and autophagic alterations in pediatric lung diseases, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia, cystic fibrosis, and viral respiratory infection, highlighting disease-specific upstream stressors and intracellular defects. Static autophagy markers cannot define functional flux, and conventional lysosomes must be distinguished from specialized lysosome-related organelles such as lamellar bodies. Finally, we discuss therapeutic opportunities and challenges, emphasizing cell-specific targeting, restoration of defined organelle defects, developmental safety, and rigorous functional validation. A developmentally informed understanding of lysosome–autophagy networks may provide new mechanistic frameworks for pediatric lung disease intervention.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5Conclusions and future perspectivesLysosomes occupy a central position at the interface of degradation, metabolism, organelle quality control, and inflammatory signaling in the developing lung. Direct pulmonary evidence supports epithelial autophagy in lung morphogenesis (7), AT-II cell autophagy-related pathways in lamellar-body maturation and surfactant homeostasis (8, 9), and the effects of experimentally altered lysosomal lipid handling on surfactant and alveolar structure (10). Disease-model studies identify context-dependent remodeling of autophagic or endolysosomal pathways in hyperoxic injury, BPD, and RSV infection (11, 19, 35, 36, 39, 40). These injury-related mechanisms should not be assumed to direct normal lung development.At the same time, the current evidence does not justify treating lysosomal dysfunction as a single uniform mechanism. The consequences of pathway perturbation depend on developmental stage, cell type, cargo, compartment, and the balance between lysosomal delivery and degradation. Static LC3-II or p62 measurements are insufficient to define flux, while pH measurements must specify the intracellular compartment. These methodological principles are essential for interpreting both experimental studies and future therapeutic trials.The most promising direction is therefore a developmentally informed, compartment-specific model of lysosomal biology. In this framework, lysosomes and lysosome-related organelles integrate metabolic and stress signals to maintain AT-II cell competence, surfactant homeostasis, mitochondrial quality, and immune function. When this adaptive network is disrupted by prematurity, hyperoxia, infection, or other stressors, impaired clearance, lipid imbalance, mitochondrial injury, and inflammatory amplification may contribute to defective alveolar and epithelial maturation. This model generates testable hypotheses without assuming that every pediatric lung phenotype is caused by a primary lysosomal defect.Future work should move from descriptive lysosomal phenotyping toward causal experiments that define the affected compartment and restore its function. Developmental timing, cell-specific delivery, dynamic flux measurements, organelle-resolved lipid and pH assays, and clinically relevant lung models will be particularly important. If these requirements are met, lysosome-centered biology may provide a tractable framework for understanding and eventually treating selected forms of pediatric lung disease.

full_text: AbstractObjectiveTo characterize the expression and evaluate the clinical utility for assessing disease severity of the serum Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6) level in children with mild and severe acute Chlamydia pneumoniae (C. pneumoniae) infection.MethodsA total of 68 hospitalized children with acute lower respiratory tract infection caused by C. pneumoniae (48 mild cases and 20 severe cases) who were admitted to Children’s Hospital of Wujiang District from May 2024 to April 2025 were enrolled, with 19 healthy children included in the control group. Serum KL-6 levels, C. pneumoniae-IgM levels, and routine laboratory indicators were measured. The correlation between the KL-6 level and clinical features was analyzed, and discriminatory performance of the KL-6 level for identifying severe C. pneumoniae infection was assessed using ROC curves.ResultsSerum KL-6 levels were significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group [303.00 (227.75, 328.25) U/mL vs. 146.50 (133.50, 164.25) U/mL, P < 0.001]. Binary logistic regression analysis indicated that KL-6 was independently associated with severe C. pneumoniae infection in children (P < 0.001), and the area under the curve (AUC) for differentiating severe infection from mild infection was 0.951 (95%CI=0.880-0.997, P<0.001). Further analysis revealed that the KL-6 level was positively correlated with the number of pulmonary lesions, the number of hospitalization days, and C. pneumoniae-IgM levels but not with other indicators.ConclusionThe serum KL-6 level can effectively reflect the degree of pulmonary parenchymal injury in children with C. pneumoniae infection and can serve as an independent biomarker for severe C. pneumoniae infection. It demonstrates high discriminatory ability for identifying severe cases and may serve as an auxiliary biomarker for assessing pulmonary parenchymal injury.Keywords: biomarker, Chlamydia pneumoniae, KL-6, pediatrics, pneumonia 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study subjectsChildren hospitalized with acute lower respiratory tract infection caused by C. pneumoniae at Children’s Hospital of Wujiang District, Suzhou (Wujiang Campus of Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Soochow University) from May 2024 to April 2025 were enrolled as the study group. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≤18 years; (2) clinical diagnosis of C. pneumoniae infection based on the Zhu Futang practice of pediatrics (8th ed., 2015), including clinical symptoms (low-grade fever, mild respiratory symptoms such as runny nose and cough, gradually worsening cough lasting 1–2 months, and rapid breathing), laboratory diagnosis (positive for serum C. pneumoniae-IgM), and imaging findings (segmental pneumonia or extensive unilateral or bilateral lesions); (3) severe cases were defined as a poor general condition, refusal to eat or dehydration, consciousness disturbance, rapid respiratory rate, cyanosis, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltration involving multiple lobes or ≥2/3 of the lung, pleural effusion, pulse oxygen saturation ≤0.92, or extrapulmonary complications; and (4) no prior medication before admission, and treatment with azithromycin or erythromycin during hospitalization.The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) had allergies, tumors, immunodeficiency, or other congenital diseases; and (2) had mixed infections with other pathogens (M. pneumoniae, influenza A virus, influenza B virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, or adenovirus). Healthy children who underwent a physical examination during the same period were selected as the control group. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of our hospital (approval number: 2023023, 2025002). No additional invasive procedures were performed for research purposes, with all data fully de-identified and a waiver of informed consent granted. All methods were performed in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki.2.2.Instruments and detection methodsSerum KL-6 levels were measured using a Fujifilm LUMIPULSE G1200 chemiluminescent immunoassay system (Rbio (Shanghai) Diagnostic Technology Co., Ltd.). Serum C. pneumoniae-IgM antibody level was measured using an iFlash 3000 chemiluminescent immunoassay system (Shenzhen YHLO Biotech Co., Ltd.). Multiplex PCR targeting Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza A virus, influenza B virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, and adenovirus was carried out using a Gentier 96R Fully Automated Medical PCR Analysis System (Xi’an Tianlong Science and Technology Co., Ltd., Xi’an).Routine blood tests (WBC count, RBC count, PLT count, neutrophil percentage, lymphocyte percentage, neutrophil absolute value, lymphocyte absolute value, and CRP level) were performed using a Mindray BC7500 automatic hematology analyzer (Shenzhen Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics Co., Ltd.). Routine biochemical parameters (ALT, LDH, and PA levels) were analyzed using a Mindray BS-2000 automatic biochemical analyzer (Shenzhen Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics Co., Ltd.). Coagulation (D-D) was assessed using a Sysmex CS-5100 automatic coagulation analyzer (Sysmex Medical Electronics (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.), and the levels of infection markers (PCT and IL-6) were measured using a Roche e411 automatic immunoassay analyzer (Roche Diagnostics (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.),RRID: SCR_018369.Imaging examinations were performed using a GE Optima 640 whole-body CT scanner (General Electric Company, USA).The KL-6 assay was performed using the Lumipulse® G KL-6 kit, with a lower limit of detection (LoD) of 1 U/mL and a coefficient of variation (CV)≤4.4%.KL-6 was quantified using the Lumipulse® G KL-6 kit (LoD: 1 U/mL; intra-assay CV ≤ 4.4%; manufacturer-recommended adult cutoff: < 500 U/mL). Multiplex PCR was performed using the Sansure Six-Pathogen Respiratory Nucleic Acid Detection Kit (intra-assay CV ≤ 5.0%) on a Gentier 96R PCR system. A result was defined as positive if typical S-shaped amplification curves were observed with Ct ≤ 40.All other routine laboratory assays were performed using original manufacturer-supplied kits. All instruments and reagents used in this study are commercially available products, not in-house research formulations.2.3.Specimen detectionAll the enrolled children underwent routine laboratory tests, including C. pneumoniae-IgM, routine blood tests, PCT, IL-6, coagulation tests, and routine biochemical tests on the day of admission, and throat swabs were collected for the nucleic acid detection of six respiratory pathogens. Children who were positive for M. pneumoniae, influenza A virus, influenza B virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, or adenovirus were excluded. Serum samples from the remaining children who were positive for C. pneumoniae-IgM were collected, frozen within 1 hour after collection, and stored at -20 °C until use. After discharge, clinical data and imaging reports were reviewed to screen specimens from children who met the inclusion criteria. Serum samples stored at -20 °C were thawed at room temperature for 30 minutes, and KL-6 levels were measured using a Fujifilm LUMIPULSE G1200 chemiluminescent immunoassay system.2.4.Data collectionOn the first day of admission, all the children with lower respiratory tract infections underwent unified routine blood tests, measurements of biochemical parameters, and assessments of infection markers. Retrospectively collected laboratory results included the WBC count, RBC count, PLT count, neutrophil percentage, lymphocyte percentage, neutrophil count, lymphocyte count, and CRP, ALT, LDH, PA, D-D, PCT, IL-6, and C. pneumoniae-IgM levels. Imaging examinations were performed on the first day of admission, and the number of infected lung segments was collected retrospectively. Hospitalization days were based on discharge records.2.5.Statistical analysisGraphPad Prism 8.0 software and IBM SPSS Statistics 22 were used for all statistical analyses. Normality testing was performed for continuous variables. Normally distributed continuous data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (x ± s) and compared using the t test. Non-normally distributed data were presented as median with interquartile range and analyzed with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U test). The chi-square test was used for comparisons of categorical variables. The diagnostic performance of each indicator was analyzed using ROC curves, and the AUC, optimal cut-off value, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and Youden’s index were calculated. The 95% confidence interval (95% CI) of AUC was calculated using the Percentile Bootstrap method, with the number of resampling iterations set to 1000. Specifically, 1000 ROC curves were generated through repeated sampling with replacement, and the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the AUC distribution were taken as the lower and upper limits of the 95% confidence interval, respectively. This method is the gold standard for confidence interval calculation in ROC analysis, which can effectively avoid the limitation of the traditional normal approximation method that the confidence interval boundaries exceed the reasonable range of 0 to 1 when the AUC is close to 1 and the sample size is relatively small. For the multivariable binary logistic regression predicting severe C. pneumoniae infection, a maximum of two predictor variables were entered into the model following the “10 events per variable” rule to mitigate overfitting risk. A two tailed adjusted P value<0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. 2.2.Instruments and detection methodsSerum KL-6 levels were measured using a Fujifilm LUMIPULSE G1200 chemiluminescent immunoassay system (Rbio (Shanghai) Diagnostic Technology Co., Ltd.). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectiveTo characterize the expression and evaluate the clinical utility for assessing disease severity of the serum Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6) level in children with mild and severe acute Chlamydia pneumoniae (C. pneumoniae) infection.MethodsA total of 68 hospitalized children with acute lower respiratory tract infection caused by C. pneumoniae (48 mild cases and 20 severe cases) who were admitted to Children’s Hospital of Wujiang District from May 2024 to April 2025 were enrolled, with 19 healthy children included in the control group. Serum KL-6 levels, C. pneumoniae-IgM levels, and routine laboratory indicators were measured. The correlation between the KL-6 level and clinical features was analyzed, and discriminatory performance of the KL-6 level for identifying severe C. pneumoniae infection was assessed using ROC curves.ResultsSerum KL-6 levels were significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group [303.00 (227.75, 328.25) U/mL vs. 146.50 (133.50, 164.25) U/mL, P < 0.001]. Binary logistic regression analysis indicated that KL-6 was independently associated with severe C. pneumoniae infection in children (P < 0.001), and the area under the curve (AUC) for differentiating severe infection from mild infection was 0.951 (95%CI=0.880-0.997, P<0.001). Further analysis revealed that the KL-6 level was positively correlated with the number of pulmonary lesions, the number of hospitalization days, and C. pneumoniae-IgM levels but not with other indicators.ConclusionThe serum KL-6 level can effectively reflect the degree of pulmonary parenchymal injury in children with C. pneumoniae infection and can serve as an independent biomarker for severe C. pneumoniae infection. It demonstrates high discriminatory ability for identifying severe cases and may serve as an auxiliary biomarker for assessing pulmonary parenchymal injury.Keywords: biomarker, Chlamydia pneumoniae, KL-6, pediatrics, pneumonia
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study subjectsChildren hospitalized with acute lower respiratory tract infection caused by C. pneumoniae at Children’s Hospital of Wujiang District, Suzhou (Wujiang Campus of Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Soochow University) from May 2024 to April 2025 were enrolled as the study group. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≤18 years; (2) clinical diagnosis of C. pneumoniae infection based on the Zhu Futang practice of pediatrics (8th ed., 2015), including clinical symptoms (low-grade fever, mild respiratory symptoms such as runny nose and cough, gradually worsening cough lasting 1–2 months, and rapid breathing), laboratory diagnosis (positive for serum C. pneumoniae-IgM), and imaging findings (segmental pneumonia or extensive unilateral or bilateral lesions); (3) severe cases were defined as a poor general condition, refusal to eat or dehydration, consciousness disturbance, rapid respiratory rate, cyanosis, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltration involving multiple lobes or ≥2/3 of the lung, pleural effusion, pulse oxygen saturation ≤0.92, or extrapulmonary complications; and (4) no prior medication before admission, and treatment with azithromycin or erythromycin during hospitalization.The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) had allergies, tumors, immunodeficiency, or other congenital diseases; and (2) had mixed infections with other pathogens (M. pneumoniae, influenza A virus, influenza B virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, or adenovirus). Healthy children who underwent a physical examination during the same period were selected as the control group. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of our hospital (approval number: 2023023, 2025002). No additional invasive procedures were performed for research purposes, with all data fully de-identified and a waiver of informed consent granted. All methods were performed in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki.2.2.Instruments and detection methodsSerum KL-6 levels were measured using a Fujifilm LUMIPULSE G1200 chemiluminescent immunoassay system (Rbio (Shanghai) Diagnostic Technology Co., Ltd.). Serum C. pneumoniae-IgM antibody level was measured using an iFlash 3000 chemiluminescent immunoassay system (Shenzhen YHLO Biotech Co., Ltd.). Multiplex PCR targeting Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza A virus, influenza B virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, and adenovirus was carried out using a Gentier 96R Fully Automated Medical PCR Analysis System (Xi’an Tianlong Science and Technology Co., Ltd., Xi’an).Routine blood tests (WBC count, RBC count, PLT count, neutrophil percentage, lymphocyte percentage, neutrophil absolute value, lymphocyte absolute value, and CRP level) were performed using a Mindray BC7500 automatic hematology analyzer (Shenzhen Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics Co., Ltd.). Routine biochemical parameters (ALT, LDH, and PA levels) were analyzed using a Mindray BS-2000 automatic biochemical analyzer (Shenzhen Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics Co., Ltd.). Coagulation (D-D) was assessed using a Sysmex CS-5100 automatic coagulation analyzer (Sysmex Medical Electronics (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.), and the levels of infection markers (PCT and IL-6) were measured using a Roche e411 automatic immunoassay analyzer (Roche Diagnostics (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.),RRID: SCR_018369.Imaging examinations were performed using a GE Optima 640 whole-body CT scanner (General Electric Company, USA).The KL-6 assay was performed using the Lumipulse® G KL-6 kit, with a lower limit of detection (LoD) of 1 U/mL and a coefficient of variation (CV)≤4.4%.KL-6 was quantified using the Lumipulse® G KL-6 kit (LoD: 1 U/mL; intra-assay CV ≤ 4.4%; manufacturer-recommended adult cutoff: < 500 U/mL). Multiplex PCR was performed using the Sansure Six-Pathogen Respiratory Nucleic Acid Detection Kit (intra-assay CV ≤ 5.0%) on a Gentier 96R PCR system. A result was defined as positive if typical S-shaped amplification curves were observed with Ct ≤ 40.All other routine laboratory assays were performed using original manufacturer-supplied kits. All instruments and reagents used in this study are commercially available products, not in-house research formulations.2.3.Specimen detectionAll the enrolled children underwent routine laboratory tests, including C. pneumoniae-IgM, routine blood tests, PCT, IL-6, coagulation tests, and routine biochemical tests on the day of admission, and throat swabs were collected for the nucleic acid detection of six respiratory pathogens. Children who were positive for M. pneumoniae, influenza A virus, influenza B virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, or adenovirus were excluded. Serum samples from the remaining children who were positive for C. pneumoniae-IgM were collected, frozen within 1 hour after collection, and stored at -20 °C until use. After discharge, clinical data and imaging reports were reviewed to screen specimens from children who met the inclusion criteria. Serum samples stored at -20 °C were thawed at room temperature for 30 minutes, and KL-6 levels were measured using a Fujifilm LUMIPULSE G1200 chemiluminescent immunoassay system.2.4.Data collectionOn the first day of admission, all the children with lower respiratory tract infections underwent unified routine blood tests, measurements of biochemical parameters, and assessments of infection markers. Retrospectively collected laboratory results included the WBC count, RBC count, PLT count, neutrophil percentage, lymphocyte percentage, neutrophil count, lymphocyte count, and CRP, ALT, LDH, PA, D-D, PCT, IL-6, and C. pneumoniae-IgM levels. Imaging examinations were performed on the first day of admission, and the number of infected lung segments was collected retrospectively. Hospitalization days were based on discharge records.2.5.Statistical analysisGraphPad Prism 8.0 software and IBM SPSS Statistics 22 were used for all statistical analyses. Normality testing was performed for continuous variables. Normally distributed continuous data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (x ± s) and compared using the t test. Non-normally distributed data were presented as median with interquartile range and analyzed with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U test). The chi-square test was used for comparisons of categorical variables. The diagnostic performance of each indicator was analyzed using ROC curves, and the AUC, optimal cut-off value, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and Youden’s index were calculated. The 95% confidence interval (95% CI) of AUC was calculated using the Percentile Bootstrap method, with the number of resampling iterations set to 1000. Specifically, 1000 ROC curves were generated through repeated sampling with replacement, and the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the AUC distribution were taken as the lower and upper limits of the 95% confidence interval, respectively. This method is the gold standard for confidence interval calculation in ROC analysis, which can effectively avoid the limitation of the traditional normal approximation method that the confidence interval boundaries exceed the reasonable range of 0 to 1 when the AUC is close to 1 and the sample size is relatively small. For the multivariable binary logistic regression predicting severe C. pneumoniae infection, a maximum of two predictor variables were entered into the model following the “10 events per variable” rule to mitigate overfitting risk. A two tailed adjusted P value<0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. 2.2.Instruments and detection methodsSerum KL-6 levels were measured using a Fujifilm LUMIPULSE G1200 chemiluminescent immunoassay system (Rbio (Shanghai) Diagnostic Technology Co., Ltd.). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionC. pneumoniae is an intracellular pathogen. The pathogenesis of C. pneumoniae infection, which involves mainly monocyte–macrophage responses, remains unclear. As carriers for the storage and transmission of pathogens, infected alveolar macrophages can migrate through the bloodstream, leading to the dissemination of Chlamydia and systemic symptoms. This mechanism is particularly crucial in C. pneumoniae infection. When C. pneumoniae infection progresses to severe cases, the extent of alveolar epithelial damage expands, potentially further exacerbating the manifestation of systemic symptoms (Tagini et al., 2025a). In recent years, the incidence of respiratory infections caused by C. pneumoniae has been increasing (Tagini et al., 2025b). The prevalence of C. pneumoniae varies among countries, ranging from 1.4% to 8.0%, and accounts for approximately 3.5% of CAP cases among Chinese children (Li et al., 2018). No significant difference in positive rates has been observed between males and females, and C. pneumoniae affects mainly children over 5 years old (Cai et al., 2022). In the early stage of acute C. pneumoniae infection, it is difficult to distinguish from infections caused by other pathogens, especially M. pneumoniae. After diagnosis, clinical laboratories need relevant indicators to assist in assessing disease severity, and laboratory indicators may also be required to monitor treatment effects (Miyashita, 2022). Therefore, how clinicians choose appropriate detection items is particularly important in the current context of tight medical resources.This study is the first to confirm that the serum KL-6 level is independently associated with severe acute C. pneumoniae infection in children (OR = 1.048, 95% CI: 1.023–1.075, P < 0.001), with an AUC of 0.951 for discriminating severe infection. These results are consistent with the role of KL-6 in other lung diseases (Hong et al., 2024): KL-6 is mainly secreted by damaged type II alveolar epithelial cells (Ishikawa et al., 2012). When C. pneumoniae infection progresses to severe disease, the range of alveolar epithelial injury expands, increasing KL-6 release, and thus it can serve as a specific biomarker for pulmonary parenchymal injury. These findings are consistent with those of studies on M. pneumoniae pneumonia (Shu et al., 2015) and RSV bronchiolitis (Kawasaki et al., 2009), suggesting that the KL-6 level is valuable for assessing lung injury caused by different pathogens in children. However, the average KL-6 expression level in patients with C. pneumoniae infection is lower than that in patients with M. pneumoniae pneumonia, possibly because C. pneumoniae infection causes mainly mild to moderate lung injury, and this study excluded children with mixed infections, reducing the inflammatory effect. Prior investigations suggest a lower pediatric reference interval for KL-6 compared to adults, with Imai et al (Imai et al., 2002) reporting a 250U/mL upper limit and Kubota & Haruta (Kubota and Haruta, 2006) proposing a 300 U/mL cutoff (mean+2SD). Our moderate-severity C. pneumoniae cohort had a median KL-6 level of 303.00 (227.75, 328.25) U/mL, and the optimal cutoff of 196.5 U/mL fell below these proposed pediatric benchmarks.This study also revealed that the KL-6 level increases with the number of lesions, directly confirming its effectiveness as a marker for the extent of lung injury, which is consistent with the conclusion proposed by Imai et al. that “elevated KL-6 reflects the degree of alveolar injury” (Imai et al., 2002). In addition, the KL-6 level is not significantly correlated with the levels of routine inflammatory indicators (e.g., CRP and PCT), indicating that KL-6 mainly reflects pulmonary parenchymal injury than the systemic inflammatory response, which can compensate for the deficiency of routine indicators in evaluating local lung injury.Of note, serum LDH was marginally lower in the severe group (230.06 ± 38.76 U/L) compared with the mild group (255.81 ± 62.44 U/L, P = 0.044).Mean LDH concentrations for both severe and mild patients fell within our healthy pediatric reference range (238.23 ± 28.63 U/L; infected vs control group, P = 0.321). The inter-group LDH difference was smaller than intrinsic biological variation among healthy children, suggesting LDH was not systemically activated in this C. pneumoniae cohort. This borderline statistical result is partly attributable to the small sample size of severe cases (n = 20) and retrospective sampling on admission. These findings fit the pathogenic features of C. pneumoniae. This obligate intracellular pathogen triggers chronic, monocyte-macrophage-predominant non-necrotic inflammation localized mainly to airway mucosa, without widespread acute pulmonary parenchymal necrosis or membrane injury, thereby limiting systemic LDH release. Multiple pediatric cohorts corroborate this view: most inflammatory markers were normal in 145 children with C. pneumoniae pneumonia (Wang et al., 2026); in a 141-patient risk model, only wheezing (OR = 15.47) and co-infection (OR = 8.25) were independent predictors of severe disease, whereas necrosis-associated markers such as LDH were excluded (Li et al., 2026). LDH therefore is unsuitable for severity assessment in isolated C. pneumoniae infection. The limitations of routine inflammatory markers further highlight the complementary diagnostic value of lung-specific KL-6 for recognition of severe infection.This study revealed that KL-6 is a serum marker of the severity of C. pneumoniae infections. If KL-6 levels continue to increase, a severe infection should be suspected, and timely intervention should be implemented to identify serious risks early. KL-6 can be used as a supplementary detection indicator for suspected severe C. pneumoniae cases, especially when routine inflammatory indicators are normal but clinical symptoms progress, helping to detect pulmonary parenchymal injury early. Given that C. pneumoniae infection is mainly mild, KL-6 does not need to be a routine screening indicator, but for children with severe symptoms such as persistent cough and rapid breathing, KL-6 detection can improve the accuracy of disease assessment and optimize the allocation of medical resources.This study has certain limitations. It was a single-center small-sample study with only 20 severe cases among 68 enrolled children, which may have affected the statistical power. Changes in KL-6 levels before and after treatment were not tracked, and thus the value of KL-6 levels in monitoring treatment effects could not be evaluated. Children with mixed infections or underlying diseases were excluded; therefore, the results may not be generalizable to patients with complex cases. Experiments to determine the molecular mechanism of action of KL-6 in alveolar epithelial cell injury were not performed; Our findings can only establish associations between KL-6 levels and disease severity, rather than causal relationships. full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionChlamydia pneumoniae (C. pneumoniae) was first isolated in 1965 from a conjunctival specimen of a child participating in a trachoma vaccine trial in Taiwan. It is among the common pathogens causing community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). C. pneumoniae is transmitted via respiratory droplets, and humans are the only known natural reservoir. C. pneumoniae infection manifests as diverse clinical phenotypes: most patients are asymptomatic or present with mild to moderate respiratory symptoms (e.g., runny nose and cough) with a long incubation period of 3–4 weeks, which is easily overlooked; a few may progress to severe pneumonia or even extrapulmonary complications. Serological tests (e.g., elevated peripheral blood IgM antibody titres) are among the gold standards for diagnosing acute C. pneumoniae infection (Miyashita, 2022). Clinicians often use routine inflammatory indicators such as the white blood cell (WBC) count, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) level, and procalcitonin (PCT) level to assess disease severity, but these indicators have limited specificity for pulmonary parenchymal injury caused by C. pneumoniae infection (Su and He, 2025).Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6) is a large molecular glycoprotein antigen that is mainly secreted by proliferating or damaged type II alveolar epithelial cells (Gao et al., 2024). KL-6 corresponds to the shed ectodomain of mucin 1 (MUC1), a transmembrane glycoprotein constitutively expressed on the apical surface of type II alveolar epithelial cells. Basal and stress-induced MUC1 synthesis, coupled with tightly regulated ectodomain shedding, are the primary determinants of circulating KL-6 concentrations under both physiological and pathological conditions (Ballester et al., 2021; Remuzgo-Martínez et al., 2021). During pulmonary inflammation or fibrotic remodeling, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-mediated proteolytic cleavage of MUC1 promotes release of the soluble KL-6 ectodomain into the alveolar space, with subsequent spillover into the systemic circulation accounting for measurable elevations in serum KL-6 levels (Zamfir et al., 2023). In 1989, the Japanese scholar Kohno and colleagues first used it to evaluate the disease activity of interstitial lung disease (ILD), and in 1999, the Japanese National Health Insurance System officially included KL-6 as a biomarker for assessing ILD disease activity (Guo et al., 2024). Current detection methods for KL-6 include ELISA, chemiluminescence, and immunoturbidimetry (Wang et al., 2023). In recent years, the clinical value of KL-6 in diagnosing various lung diseases has been confirmed: it can predict the risk of severe COVID-19 pneumonia (Snopkowska Lesniak et al., 2025), is correlated with in-hospital mortality in patients with CAP (Lu et al., 2023; Heltborg et al., 2024), and can be used to monitor disease progression in patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced pneumonia (Matsukane et al., 2024). However, the expression pattern of KL-6, the correlation of the KL-6 level with disease severity, and discriminatory performance of the KL-6 level for acute C. pneumoniae infection in children remain unclear, with few relevant studies (Achille et al., 2025).C. pneumoniae infection is an important cause of CAP in children (Ma et al., 2022; Basile and Sandelich, 2025). Due to the nonspecific symptoms and insufficient sensitivity of routine inflammatory indicators for pulmonary parenchymal injury, biomarkers that can accurately reflect alveolar epithelial injury caused by C. pneumoniae infection are urgently needed. C. pneumoniae infection exacerbates alveolar epithelial injury via characteristic monocyte-macrophage-mediated inflammatory responses, thereby driving measurable elevations in circulating KL-6 levels. This study aimed to analyze the differences in serum KL-6 levels between children with mild and severe acute C. pneumoniae infection, explore its clinical value as an auxiliary indicator for assessing severe infection and pulmonary parenchymal injury, and provide a basis for the rational selection of clinical detection items. 2.1.Study subjectsChildren hospitalized with acute lower respiratory tract infection caused by C. pneumoniae at Children’s Hospital of Wujiang District, Suzhou (Wujiang Campus of Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Soochow University) from May 2024 to April 2025 were enrolled as the study group. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≤18 years; (2) clinical diagnosis of C. pneumoniae infection based on the Zhu Futang practice of pediatrics (8th ed., 2015), including clinical symptoms (low-grade fever, mild respiratory symptoms such as runny nose and cough, gradually worsening cough lasting 1–2 months, and rapid breathing), laboratory diagnosis (positive for serum C. pneumoniae-IgM), and imaging findings (segmental pneumonia or extensive unilateral or bilateral lesions); (3) severe cases were defined as a poor general condition, refusal to eat or dehydration, consciousness disturbance, rapid respiratory rate, cyanosis, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltration involving multiple lobes or ≥2/3 of the lung, pleural effusion, pulse oxygen saturation ≤0.92, or extrapulmonary complications; and (4) no prior medication before admission, and treatment with azithromycin or erythromycin during hospitalization.The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) had allergies, tumors, immunodeficiency, or other congenital diseases; and (2) had mixed infections with other pathogens (M. pneumoniae, influenza A virus, influenza B virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, or adenovirus). Healthy children who underwent a physical examination during the same period were selected as the control group. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of our hospital (approval number: 2023023, 2025002). No additional invasive procedures were performed for research purposes, with all data fully de-identified and a waiver of informed consent granted. All methods were performed in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki. 2.3.Specimen detectionAll the enrolled children underwent routine laboratory tests, including C. pneumoniae-IgM, routine blood tests, PCT, IL-6, coagulation tests, and routine biochemical tests on the day of admission, and throat swabs were collected for the nucleic acid detection of six respiratory pathogens. title: Size, cytopathic effects, and prevalence of Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV in healthcare settings
abstract: Airborne transmission of respiratory viruses in healthcare settings is difficult to assess, particularly with respect to the size and viability of virus-containing aerosols. Most field studies rely on molecular detection, which limits inference about the infectiousness of virus. In this study we collected size-resolved airborne samples in a dental clinic and hospital during the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season using a BC (BioCascade)-BioSpot VIVAS (Viable Virus Aerosol Sampler). We analyzed these samples by RT-PCR and culture-based assays for influenza A, influenza B, SARS-CoV-2, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Viral RNA was detected in 11.1% of the 81 sampling events, with the highest positivity (25%) observed in pulmonary unit patient rooms. When influenza and SARS-CoV-2 RNA were detected, all of these detections occurred in the 4-10 μm size fraction, whereas all RSV RNA was detected in the <1.5 μm size fraction. Cell culture assays confirmed the presence of viable influenza in the samples that were positive by RT-PCR. Plaques were only observed for influenza A viral positive samples at the ‘neat’ or undiluted rate, whereas RSV and SARS-CoV-2 did not produce cytopathic effects in the cell culture assays. These findings highlight virus-specific differences in aerosol size distributions and the challenges of recovering viable virus from field-collected bioaerosols in healthcare environments.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to assess airborne transmission of respiratory viruses in healthcare settings, focusing on the size and viability of virus-containing aerosols. Airborne samples were collected in a dental clinic and hospital during the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season using a BC-BioSpot VIVAS sampler. Viral RNA was detected in 11.1% of 81 sampling events, with the highest positivity in pulmonary unit patient rooms. RSV RNA was consistently found in the <1.5 μm size fraction, while influenza and SARS-CoV-2 RNA were detected in the 4-10 μm size fraction. Cell culture assays confirmed the presence of viable influenza in RT-PCR-positive samples, but no cytopathic effects were observed for RSV or SARS-CoV-2. These results emphasize virus-specific differences in aerosol size distributions and the challenges of recovering viable virus from field samples. The study provides insights into the behavior of RSV in healthcare environments but does not address limitations or evidence strength.

abstract_zh: 在医疗保健环境中评估呼吸道病毒气溶胶的传播性(传播)具有挑战性,尤其是在病毒气溶胶的大小和活性方面。大多数现场研究依赖于分子检测,这限制了对病毒传染性的推断。本研究在2024-2025年呼吸道病毒季节期间,使用BC(BioCascade)-BioSpot VIVAS(可培养病毒气溶胶采样器)在牙科诊所和医院中收集了具有粒径分辨率的空气样本。我们通过RT-PCR和基于培养的检测方法分析了这些样本,以检测流感A型、流感B型、SARS-CoV-2和呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)。在81次采样事件中,有11.1%的样本检测到病毒RNA,其中肺病单元病房的阳性率最高(25%)。当检测到流感和SARS-CoV-2的RNA时,所有检测均发生在4-10 μm粒径组分中,而所有RSV RNA均检测到在<1.5 μm粒径组分中。细胞培养检测证实了通过RT-PCR检测为阳性的样本中存在可培养的流感病毒。仅在流感A型病毒阳性样本中观察到斑块,而RSV和SARS-CoV-2在细胞培养检测中未产生细胞病变效应。这些发现突显了不同病毒在气溶胶粒径分布上的特异性差异,以及在医疗保健环境中从现场收集的生物气溶胶中回收活性病毒的挑战。
